Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models

Minhua Lin Affiliation: The Pennsylvania State University    Zijun Wang Affiliation: UC Santa Cruz    Zewen Liu Affiliation: Emory University    Zhaotian Weng Affiliation: UC Santa Barbara    Bing He Affiliation: Amazon{mfl5681,szw494}@psu.edu; {luhanqin}@amazon.com    Zhan Shi Affiliation: Amazon{mfl5681,szw494}@psu.edu; {luhanqin}@amazon.com    Benoit Dumoulin Affiliation: Amazon{mfl5681,szw494}@psu.edu; {luhanqin}@amazon.com    Xiang Zhang Affiliation: The Pennsylvania State University    Suhang Wang Affiliation: The Pennsylvania State University    Hanqing Lu Affiliation: Amazon{mfl5681,szw494}@psu.edu; {luhanqin}@amazon.com
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) Radford et al. (2018); Radford et al. (2019); Touvron et al. (2023) are increasingly being adopted as agents for automated AI research (AutoResearch) Karpathy (2026), where they propose ideas, implement changes, and execute experiments Si et al. (2026); Novikov et al. (2025). A promising application is language-model development (LM development), where agents explore architectural, optimization, and training choices and measure their effects on model performance Chi et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2026a). These experiments generate feedback that could help LLMs learn how to improve language models. Developing this capability could accelerate model development and support progress toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) Chi et al. (2026) (Fig. 1(a)).

Despite these advances, deciding what to try, i.e., research judgment, remains a bottleneck for LLM-based research agents. Agents can implement and execute complex experiments, yet still struggle to identify changes that yield meaningful improvements Li et al. (2026); Si et al. (2026); Chi et al. (2026). In LM development, effective choices depend on the target model and its training configuration: a change that benefits one setting may not benefit another. With expensive training experiments, selecting promising changes is essential to making effective use of limited experimental resources. We therefore ask: how can language models learn to make better model-improvement decisions and transfer this capability to new models and training configurations?

A natural way to improve research judgment is to learn from past experiments. Experimental records can inform an LLM’s decisions through in-context learning (ICL) Brown et al. (2020); Novikov et al. (2025); Si et al. (2026), and can also improve predictions of experimental outcomes and the selection of promising proposals Wang et al. (2026b). This suggests using experimental knowledge as feedback for parameter learning to improve an LLM’s proposal-generation capability beyond in-context learning. However, learning from this feedback raises two key challenges (Fig. 1(b)-(c)).

First, how can we obtain cheap and scalable training feedback? Training LLMs with reinforcement learning (RL) to generate better proposals requires feedback on numerous sampled proposals. The most direct feedback comes from executing each proposal and measuring its outcome Si et al. (2026), but this requires costly model-training runs. For example, training a 486M-parameter model on 8B tokens takes approximately 45 B200 GPU-hours. A GRPO-style RL Shao et al. (2024) setup with 100 updates, 32 training states per update, and 8 proposals per state would require 25,600 proposal evaluations. Executing these proposals at the same per-run cost would consume approximately 1,152,000 GPU-hours, costing over $16 million. This motivates low-cost surrogate feedback without executing every proposal. Second, how can we keep surrogate feedback reliable as learning progresses? Accurate predictions on past experiments do not ensure reliable feedback throughout training. As learning changes which proposals the LLM generates, the surrogate must evaluate proposals that its experimental records may not cover. RL may then favor overestimated proposals, increasing surrogate rewards without corresponding real gains Gao et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2026). A scalable learning approach must therefore keep its feedback grounded in real outcomes on the proposals the current LLM generates.

To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, a framework that trains LLMs with RL to generate effective proposals for LM development. To obtain cheap and scalable training signals, we use a frozen LLM as a research world model (RWM) Wang et al. (2026b) to predict experimental gains relative to a reference configuration without executing proposals. Grounded in an initial set of real experimental records provided as in-context knowledge, the RWM supplies predicted gains for constructing RL rewards Yu et al. (2026). To keep this feedback reliable as training progresses, we introduce on-policy calibration: we periodically execute a subset of the current policy’s proposals that the RWM ranks highly and incorporate their measured outcomes into its in-context knowledge. This targets real execution at proposals favored by RL, where overestimation can misdirect learning, and helps maintain prediction reliability as LLMs’ proposals change.

Our contributions are: (i) Method. We propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL using RWM-based rewards grounded in real records and calibrated through targeted real execution; (ii) Experiments. Extensive real-execution experiments on held-out environments show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform frontier models such as GPT-6-sol and surpass baselines leveraging past experimental records at lower data-generation cost; (iii) Analysis. We show that RWM-based feedback provides informative rankings of proposal gains, while on-policy calibration mitigates overestimation and largely preserves ranking quality as training progresses, unlike a fixed-record RWM that eventually performs worse than random.

2 Related Work

AutoResearch with LLM Agents. AutoResearch aims to automate empirical AI research through iterative idea generation, experimental implementation, execution, and analysis. Early work shows LLM agents’ ability to generate research ideas and conduct end-to-end experiments Baek et al. (2025); Si et al. (2025); Lu et al. (2024); Weng et al. (2026), with benchmarks evaluating these capabilities in machine-learning engineering and AI R&D Huang et al. (2024); Chan et al. (2025); Wijk et al. (2025); Chi et al. (2026). To improve research outcomes, some methods iterate on candidate solutions with execution feedback while keeping the underlying agent fixed Jiang et al. (2025); Novikov et al. (2025); Karpathy (2026). Others instead train the agent on execution feedback, for machine-learning engineering Yang et al. (2026a) and LLM model development Si et al. (2026). However, these methods rely on costly real execution to obtain training signals, limiting learning at scale. In contrast, we train LLMs with feedback from a world model that predicts experimental outcomes, enabling scalable learning with fewer real executions. Full details of related works are in Appendix A.

3 Methodology

In this section, we present LM2LM. We first formalize AutoResearch for LM development and motivate RL-based proposer training (Sec. 3.1). To provide scalable feedback, we use a frozen LLM as a research world model (RWM) to predict experimental gains without executing proposals, and use its predictions as RL rewards (Sec. 3.2). To maintain reliable feedback as the proposer evolves, we periodically execute high-rated proposals from the current policy and incorporate their measured outcomes into the RWM’s context (Sec. 3.3). An overview of LM2LM is shown in Fig. 2.

3.1 Preliminaries

AutoResearch for LM Development. We consider a set of AutoResearch tasks ℰ\mathcal{E}, where each task e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} seeks to improve a target language model by modifying its architecture, training objective, or optimization. Each task specifies a model family, model size, pretraining budget, and a reference configuration with validation loss beb_{e}.

A research campaign on task ee involves two LLM-based roles: a proposer πθ\pi_{\theta}, which generates proposals, and a builder ℬ\mathcal{B}, which translates them into executable modifications to the reference configuration. A campaign proceeds through repeated proposal-and-execution steps. At step tt, the proposer observes the research state st=(e,ht)s_{t}=(e,h_{t}), where hth_{t} records the proposals executed in previous steps and their measured outcomes, and generates a proposal at∼πθ(⋅∣st)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). The builder implements ata_{t}, and the resulting training run yields validation loss ℓt\ell_{t}. The experimental gain is defined as

g⁡(st,at)=be−ℓt,g(s_{t},a_{t})=b_{e}-\ell_{t}, (1)

where g⁡(st,at)>0g(s_{t},a_{t})>0 indicates an improvement over the reference configuration. The proposal and its measured outcome are appended to the history, producing ht+1h_{t+1} and the next research state st+1=(e,ht+1)s_{t+1}=(e,h_{t+1}).

Problem Statement. An AutoResearch campaign consists of a sequence of research steps, where each step requires the proposer to decide what proposal to explore next based on the current task and previous experimental outcomes. In this paper, our goal is then to improve this decision-making capability by training a proposer πθ\pi_{\theta} to generate proposals with high experimental gain at each step.

Formally, let ℰtrain\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{train}} and ℰtest\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{test}} denote disjoint sets of training and held-out tasks, respectively, and let μtrain\mu_{\mathrm{train}} and μtest\mu_{\mathrm{test}} denote the corresponding distributions over research states s=(e,h)s=(e,h). For ν∈{train,test}\nu\in\{\mathrm{train},\mathrm{test}\}, we define the expected experimental gain as

Jν(θ)=𝔼s∼μν,a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[g(s,a)],J_{\nu}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mu_{\nu},\,a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)}\left[g(s,a)\right], (2)

where Jν​(θ)J_{\nu}(\theta) measures the expected experimental gain of proposals generated by πθ\pi_{\theta} across research states sampled from μν\mu_{\nu}. We seek to maximize Jtrain​(θ)J_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta) using training tasks, with the aim of achieving high Jtest​(θ)J_{\mathrm{test}}(\theta) on held-out tasks.

RL with Experimental Feedback. Since the experimental gain g⁡(s,a)g(s,a) directly measures the quality of a proposal, it can serve as a verifiable reward, making reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) a natural approach to optimizing Jtrain​(θ)J_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta) Lambert et al. (2025). A representative algorithm is DAPO Yu et al. (2026): for a state s∼μtrains\sim\mu_{\mathrm{train}}, it samples a group of GG proposals {ai}i=1G\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the current policy πθold(⋅∣s)\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid s), scores them with rewards {Ri}i=1G\{R_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}, and maximizes

𝒥DAPO(θ)=𝔼[\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Big[ 1∑i|ai|∑i=1G∑k=1|ai|\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{\sum_{i}|a_{i}|}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^{|a_{i}|} (3)
min(ρi,kA^i,ρ¯i,kA^i)],\displaystyle\min\big(\rho_{i,k}\hat{A}_{i},\,\bar{\rho}_{i,k}\hat{A}_{i}\big)\Big],

where |ai||a_{i}| is the number of tokens in aia_{i}, ρi,k=πθ​(ai,k∣s,ai,<k)/πθold​(ai,k∣s,ai,<k)\rho_{i,k}=\pi_{\theta}(a_{i,k}\mid s,a_{i,<k})/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,k}\mid s,a_{i,<k}) is the token-level probability ratio, ρ¯i,k=clip⁡(ρi,k,1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)\bar{\rho}_{i,k}=\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,k},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}), and the advantage A^i=(Ri−mean⁡({Rj}j=1G))/std⁡({Rj}j=1G)\hat{A}_{i}=\big(R_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})\big)/\mathrm{std}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}). Groups with no reward variation are discarded.

3.2 Scalable Feedback: Research World Model as the Verifier

RLVR typically relies on inexpensive verification, e.g., checking the correctness of a mathematical answer Cobbe et al. (2021). However, directly applying RLVR to AutoResearch for LM development is computationally expensive, as evaluating each proposal requires training the target model to measure its experimental gain. Since RL samples numerous proposals across research states and training updates, obtaining execution-based rewards at scale becomes prohibitively costly. To address this challenge, we use a research world model (RWM) to predict experimental gains without executing every proposal, and train the proposer with DAPO on rewards built from these predictions.

Research World Model. An RWM predicts the outcomes of AI research experiments without executing them Wang et al. (2026b). We instantiate it as a frozen LLM WW. To improve prediction reliability, we ground it in real experimental records. Specifically, we collect N0N_{0} experimental records from training tasks to form the initial record set M0M_{0}. Each record (e,a,g)(e,a,g) contains a task, an executed proposal, and its measured gain. Formally, given a task ee, proposal aa, and experimental records MM, the RWM predicts the experimental gain g^​(e,a,M)\hat{g}(e,a;M) as

g^​(e,a,M)=W⁡(e,a,M),\hat{g}(e,a;M)=W(e,a;M), (4)

where MM is provided as in-context evidence. Thus, evaluating a proposal requires only an LLM call rather than a model-training run.

Reward Design. A straightforward approach is to use RWM-predicted gains directly as RL rewards. This poses two challenges. First, predicted gains vary in scale across tasks and may contain extreme values, allowing tasks with larger gain scales or a few extreme predictions to dominate policy optimization. Second, high predicted gains do not necessarily imply useful proposals, as proposals may be invalid, repetitive, or insufficiently diverse.

To address the first challenge, we normalize predicted gains by a task-specific scale τe\tau_{e} and clip them at a threshold cc:

r⁡(s,a,M)=clip⁡(g^​(e,a,M)/τe,−c,c),r(s,a;M)=\mathrm{clip}\big(\hat{g}(e,a;M)/\tau_{e},\,-c,\,c\big), (5)

where ee is the task associated with research state ss, and τe\tau_{e} is determined by reference seed noise and the dispersion of RWM-predicted gains. Normalization makes rewards comparable across tasks, while clipping limits the influence of extreme predictions on policy updates.

To address the second challenge, we incorporate proposal validity, novelty, and diversity into the final rewards. For a group of GG proposals sampled from state ss, a proposal is invalid if it cannot be implemented by the builder, repeated if it reproduces the reference configuration or a proposal in the history hh, and valid otherwise. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} denote the set of valid proposals within the group. We assign

Ri={r⁡(s,ai,M)+bi,ai∈𝒱,minj∈𝒱⁡Rj−δ,ai​ repeated,−c,ai​ invalid,R_{i}=\begin{cases}r(s,a_{i};M)+b_{i},&a_{i}\in\mathcal{V},\\[2.0pt] \min_{j\in\mathcal{V}}R_{j}-\delta,&a_{i}\text{ repeated},\\[2.0pt] -c,&a_{i}\text{ invalid},\end{cases} (6)

where δ>0\delta>0 is a repetition margin and bi=λ​σG​d~ib_{i}=\lambda\sigma_{G}\tilde{d}_{i} is a diversity bonus. Here, di=1/nid_{i}=1/n_{i}, where nin_{i} is the number of valid proposals sharing the same mechanism direction as aia_{i} within the group; d~i\tilde{d}_{i} is the within-group standardized value of did_{i}, σG\sigma_{G} is the standard deviation of normalized predicted rewards within the group, and λ\lambda controls the bonus strength. The diversity bonus favors less common mechanism directions to encourage broader exploration during RL. Repeated proposals provide no new experimental information but may receive high predicted gains, so δ\delta ranks them below all valid proposals. More reward details are in Appendix B.1.

Policy Optimization. With the rewards in Eq. (6), we train the proposer using DAPO (Eq. (3)). Since rewards are already normalized by τe\tau_{e} to be comparable across tasks, we use group-mean-centered advantages A^i=Ri−mean⁡({Rj}j=1G)\hat{A}_{i}=R_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}) without dividing by the group’s standard deviation Liu et al. (2025), preserving reward dispersion across groups.

Beyond providing RL rewards, the RWM also enables low-cost expansion of RL training states. Each RL training state s=(e,h)s=(e,h) pairs a training task ee with a history hh sampled from {(e′,a,g)∈𝒫:e′=e}\{(e^{\prime},a,g)\in\mathcal{P}:e^{\prime}=e\}, where the record pool 𝒫\mathcal{P} is initialized as M0M_{0}. Since M0M_{0} contains only a few records per task and scaling up 𝒫\mathcal{P} with real outcomes requires costly execution, we periodically add the state–proposal pairs 𝒟\mathcal{D} sampled during RL to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, with their RWM-predicted gains as synthetic outcomes (Appendix B.2):

𝒫←𝒫∪{(e,a,g^​(e,a,M)):((e,h),a)∈𝒟}.\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\cup\big\{\big(e,a,\hat{g}(e,a;M)\big):\big((e,h),a\big)\in\mathcal{D}\big\}. (7)

Thus, both RWM-based rewards and synthetic training states enable scalable RL without executing every sampled proposal.

3.3 Reliable Feedback: On-Policy Calibration of the RWM

Prediction Bias under Policy Shift. While the RWM provides scalable feedback, RL increasingly favors highly rated proposals that may not be adequately covered by the initial records M0M_{0}, making it susceptible to reward overoptimization Gao et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2026). To characterize this risk, we decompose the normalized real objective as

J¯​(θ)=𝔼⁡[r⁡(s,a,M)]⏟J^M​(θ)+𝔼⁡[g¯​(s,a)−r⁡(s,a,M)]⏟ΔM​(θ),\bar{J}(\theta)=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[r(s,a;M)\big]}_{\hat{J}_{M}(\theta)}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\bar{g}(s,a)-r(s,a;M)\big]}_{\Delta_{M}(\theta)}, (8)

where J¯​(θ)=𝔼​[g¯​(s,a)]\bar{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[\bar{g}(s,a)], g¯​(s,a)=clip⁡(g⁡(s,a)/τe,−c,c)\bar{g}(s,a)=\mathrm{clip}(g(s,a)/\tau_{e},-c,c), and the expectations are over s∼μtrains\sim\mu_{\mathrm{train}} and a∼πθ(⋅∣s)a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s). Here, J^M​(θ)\hat{J}_{M}(\theta) is the expected normalized predicted gain, and ΔM​(θ)\Delta_{M}(\theta) is its prediction bias under the current proposer. As RL optimizes RWM-based rewards without observing this bias, J^M\hat{J}_{M} may increase without a corresponding increase in J¯\bar{J}.

Targeted Calibration with Real Execution. To mitigate this risk, we introduce on-policy calibration: rather than keeping the RWM’s records fixed, LM2LM periodically executes high-rated proposals from the current proposer and incorporates their real outcomes into the records to improve RWM predictions as the proposer evolves.

Specifically, at each update point uu, let 𝒞u\mathcal{C}_{u} denote the current proposer’s samples on training states, excluding proposals whose outcomes are already in MuM_{u}. We select BuB_{u} high-rated proposals:

𝒬u=arg​max𝒬⊆𝒞u,|𝒬|=Bu∑(s,a)∈𝒬r(s,a;Mu).\mathcal{Q}_{u}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{u},\;|\mathcal{Q}|=B_{u}}\;\sum_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{Q}}r(s,a;M_{u}). (9)

The builder implements and executes these proposals, and their measured outcomes are added to the records:

Mu+1=Mu∪{(e,a,g⁡(s,a)):(s,a)∈𝒬u},M_{u+1}=M_{u}\cup\big\{(e,a,g(s,a)):(s,a)\in\mathcal{Q}_{u}\big\}, (10)

where ee is the task of ss. Subsequent RL steps compute rewards with W⁡(⋅,Mu+1)W(\cdot\,;M_{u+1}). Calibration occurs between RL training segments, keeping the RWM feedback fixed within each segment.

Since calibration updates the RWM through in-context records without retraining, it requires only ∑u=0U−1Bu\sum_{u=0}^{U-1}B_{u} additional real executions, independent of the number of proposals sampled during RL. The training algorithm is summarized in Alg. 1.

4 Experiments

In this section, we first compare LM2LM with baselines on proposal quality and data-generation cost (Sec. 4.2) and evaluate its generalization to an unseen model family (Sec. 4.3). We then conduct ablation studies to understand the contribution of on-policy calibration (Sec. 4.4) and analyze why RWM feedback can guide RL and how calibration sustains it (Sec. 4.5).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Environments. We construct language-model training environments spanning four autoregressive (AR) families: OLMo-3 Olmo et al. (2025), Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025), NanoChat Karpathy (2025), and Marin Hall et al. (2025); and four diffusion families: E2D2-SW, E2D2 Arriola et al. (2026), MDM Nie et al. (2025), and BD3LM Arriola et al. (2025). Each task specifies a model family, model size, training budget, and reference training recipe. Each experiment trains the target model from scratch. Further details are in Appendix C.1.

Data Construction. We split the tasks into 40 training and 10 held-out tasks. We curate and execute 300 proposals from a library of training-recipe mechanisms on the training tasks, yielding 300 experimental records. Of these, 100 serve as the initial records M0M_{0} of LM2LM, grounding the RWM. We construct initial RL training states s=(e,h)s=(e,h) with histories hh containing 0–8 records of task ee from M0M_{0}, expanded during RL (Eq. (7)). For evaluation, we construct 60 AR and 18 diffusion held-out research states using only real experimental histories. More details are in Appendix C.2.

Baselines. We compare LM2LM with training-free and fine-tuning-based methods. (i) Training-free proposers: We evaluate LM2LM’s base model and a frontier LLM (GPT-6-sol) in both zero-shot and in-context learning (ICL) settings. For ICL, we use the above 300 experimental records as in-context examples. (ii) Fine-tuned proposers: SFT fine-tunes the base model on 300 (state, proposal) pairs constructed from the same records, and RFT-Real applies rejection-sampling fine-tuning Yuan et al. (2023), keeping only the pairs whose proposals have positive measured gains. Both use the same base model and builder as LM2LM.

Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate proposers on held-out research states through real execution, with each proposer generating four proposals per state. We measure experimental gains using validation bits per byte (BPB) for AR models and negative log-likelihood (NLL) for diffusion models. We report Avg@4, Best@4, negative-gain rate (Neg.), and pairwise win rates based on Avg@4. To assess efficiency, we measure data-generation cost and time, including real execution and RWM prediction costs. GPU time is priced at $14.208 per B200 GPU-hour and RWM calls at GPT-6-sol token rates. More details are in Appendix D.

Implementation Details. We use Qwen3.8-27B Qwen Team (2026) as the proposer backbone, GPT-6-sol OpenAI (2026b) as the RWM, and GPT-6-astra OpenAI (2026a) as the builder, both at high reasoning effort. We run DAPO for 96 steps, refreshing rollouts every 8 steps with 256 training states and G=8G=8 proposals per state, and clipping rewards at c=6c=6. Starting with N0=100N_{0}=100 initial experimental records, we calibrate the RWM three times (U=3U=3), after steps 16, 40, and 64, by executing proposals selected using Eq. (9), so that LM2LM uses 200 real runs by default and each of the four training segments has a fixed RWM reward function. Unless otherwise specified, we report results at step 96. More details are in Appendix E.

4.2 Main Comparison with Baselines

Main Results. We compare LM2LM with baselines on proposal quality across held-out research states, following the evaluation protocol in Sec. 4.1. Table 1 reports the results. We observe: (i) Past experimental experience helps, but how it is used matters. With 300 experimental records, Base-ICL improves Avg@4 over Base from −7.94-7.94 to 4.044.04 on AR tasks and from −4.18-4.18 to 4.034.03 on diffusion tasks, demonstrating the value of past experimental experience. In contrast, SFT and RFT-Real fail to consistently improve proposal quality, suggesting that directly fine-tuning on a few hundred past proposals is insufficient to learn effective proposal generation. (ii) LM2LM outperforms all baselines. It achieves the highest Avg@4 and Best@4 on both AR (17.06/23.40) and diffusion (7.10/9.93) tasks, outperforming Base on 93.3% and 100% of states, respectively. This validates LM2LM’s effectiveness. (iii) RL reduces harmful proposals while enabling larger gains. Compared with Base, LM2LM reduces negative-gain proposals from 70.4% to 39.2% on AR tasks and from 59.7% to 7.6% on diffusion tasks. Despite a higher negative-gain rate than GPT-6-sol-ICL on AR tasks (39.2% vs. 29.6%), LM2LM achieves substantially higher Avg@4 (17.06 vs. 6.15), suggesting that it explores higher-gain proposals rather than simply avoiding negative outcomes.

Cost Efficiency. We compare all methods in terms of Avg@4 and Best@4 versus data-generation cost and time. For ICL baselines, we vary the number of in-context records K∈{0,100,150,200,300}K\in\{0,100,150,200,300\}. For LM2LM, we evaluate checkpoints at steps 16, 40, 64, 96, and 128, corresponding to RWM records M0M_{0} through M4M_{4}. Figure 3 reports Avg@4 results, with Best@4 results in Appendix G.1. We observe that (i) LM2LM achieves larger gains with fewer real executions. At step 96 (M3M_{3}), LM2LM achieves Avg@4 of 17.06 and 7.10 on AR and diffusion tasks, respectively, outperforming ICL with K=200K=200 at comparable data-generation cost ($40.1k vs. $39.5k). Compared with ICL at K=300K=300, it achieves higher gains with only 200 real runs, reducing data-generation cost and time by approximately 33% ($40.1k vs. $60.0k; 343 vs. 510 hours). Even including RL training, its total cost remains lower than ICL with K=300K=300 ($56.1k vs. $60.0k), as detailed in Appendix G.2. (ii) LM2LM improves further at limited additional cost as training progresses. Between steps 40 and 96, LM2LM improves Avg@4 from 10.85 to 17.06 on AR tasks and from 2.28 to 7.10 on diffusion tasks. This requires only $11.8k in additional data-generation cost, providing RWM rewards for over 14k sampled proposals with just 69 additional calibration records. These results show how LM2LM scales training feedback with limited real execution.

4.3 Generalization to Unseen Model Families

We further evaluate whether LM2LM generalizes to an unseen model family. Specifically, we hold out the entire Qwen3 family and train the proposer on the remaining families, excluding all Qwen3 records from training and RWM grounding. (i) LM2LM generalizes to unseen model families. Without Qwen3 records, LM2LM achieves Avg@4 and Best@4 of 53.72 and 86.69, substantially outperforming the strongest baseline (21.63 and 25.27 for GPT-6-sol-ICL), demonstrating its ability to generate effective proposals for an unseen model family. (ii) Out-of-family in-context records provide limited benefits. Base-ICL performs similarly to Base (2.97 vs. 3.53 Avg@4), while GPT-6-sol-ICL only slightly improves over GPT-6-sol (21.63 vs. 20.19). This suggests that directly using out-of-family records offers limited benefits, highlighting the advantage of LM2LM’s RWM-based RL.

4.4 Ablation Studies

To understand the contributions of on-policy calibration and the impact of its proposal selection strategy, we conduct ablation studies by comparing LM2LM with variants that differ only in how the RWM records are constructed, with all other settings following Sec. 4.1.

Impact of On-Policy Calibration. We compare LM2LM with two static variants whose records stay fixed: M0M_{0} (100 initial records) and M0′M_{0}^{\prime} (M0M_{0} plus 100 random records, matching LM2LM’s 200 real runs). As shown in Fig. 4(a), LM2LM achieves higher AR Avg@4 and Best@4 than both variants, and outperforms M0M_{0} and M0′M_{0}^{\prime} in Avg@4 on 74.2% and 70.0% of the held-out AR states, respectively. With the same budget of 200 real runs, calibration outperforms adding random records (17.06 vs. 14.76 Avg@4), highlighting the importance of proposal selection for RWM grounding.

Impact of Calibration Strategy. We further assess the impact of top-rated proposal selection in Eq. (9) by comparing LM2LM with a variant that uniformly samples valid proposals whose outcomes are not yet in the records, while keeping the same initial records and three calibration rounds (200 real runs). As shown in Fig. 4(b), random calibration lowers AR Avg@4 and Best@4 from 17.06 and 23.40 to 10.84 and 18.60. We attribute this to top-rated selection correcting overestimated changes that RL is about to reinforce, whereas random selection can miss them or add misleading records. Case studies are in Appendix H.

4.5 In-depth Dissection of LM2LM

We further analyze why RWM feedback can guide RL and how calibration keeps it reliable. For this analysis, we extend training from 96 to 128 steps with a fourth calibration of LM2LM (236 real runs) and compare it with the static variant whose RWM keeps M0M_{0} throughout; each variant is scored by the RWM it is trained with.

Why Can RWM Feedback Guide RL? We examine the alignment between RWM-predicted and real-execution feedback by measuring the cosine similarity of group-relative advantages and the within-state pairwise ranking accuracy over four executed proposals per held-out AR research state. As shown in Figs. 5(a) and (b), LM2LM maintains advantage cosine of 0.50–0.71 and pairwise accuracy of 0.61–0.69, above chance levels of 0 and 0.5. Since DAPO optimizes group-relative advantages, this indicates that the RWM provides informative relative feedback for policy optimization.

How Does On-Policy Calibration Help? To understand the gains from calibration in Sec. 4.4, we examine how the feedback of the static variant evolves as RL changes the proposer’s outputs (Fig. 5). We observe that (i) Calibration maintains reliable relative feedback. As shown in Fig. 5(a), the static RWM’s advantage cosine declines from 0.69 at step 16 to −0.42-0.42 at step 128, so its predicted advantages become negatively aligned with real ones, whereas LM2LM keeps it positive. Likewise, its pairwise accuracy drops from 0.72 to 0.37, below chance (0.5), while LM2LM maintains 0.61 (Fig. 5(b)). We further observe that scoring the same LM2LM proposals with M0M_{0} instead of calibrated records lowers pairwise accuracy from 0.61 to 0.46 at step 96 (Appendix I.2). These results indicate that on-policy calibration keeps the predicted advantages that DAPO optimizes aligned with real ones. (ii) Calibration limits reward overestimation. As shown in Fig. 5(c), the predicted–real reward gap of the static RWM rises sharply after step 64, reaching about 2.0 at step 96, whereas LM2LM’s gap stays below 1 and decreases from 0.85 at step 96 to 0.17 at step 128 after the fourth calibration. Thus, calibration also keeps predicted rewards close to real ones, mitigating reward overoptimization Gao et al. (2023). For example, our case studies in Appendix I.3 show that the initial RWM overestimates a NanoChat optimizer change (predicted +0.7+0.7 to +1.25+1.25 vs. real −1.46-1.46), so the static variant raises its share of NanoChat training proposals from 30% to 79% by step 64. In contrast, the first calibration of LM2LM adds its real outcomes to the records, and the share falls to 8%. More metrics and case studies are in Appendix I.

5 Conclusion

We presented LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective proposals for LM development, using a frozen LLM grounded in real experimental records as an RWM and keeping it reliable through on-policy calibration. Extensive experiments across autoregressive and diffusion LM environments show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform frontier models such as GPT-6-sol and achieve higher gains than baselines leveraging past experimental records at lower data-generation cost. Our analysis shows that RWM-based feedback provides informative rankings of proposal gains, while on-policy calibration mitigates reward overestimation and preserves ranking quality as training progresses. These findings highlight RWM-guided RL as a promising paradigm for learning research judgment from experimental feedback, offering a potential path toward RSI.

6 Limitations

Our study focuses on proposal-level improvements in LM development rather than end-to-end research campaigns. Although the RWM provides informative rankings and substantially reduces the need for real execution during RL, its predictions remain imperfect, and on-policy calibration still requires a limited number of additional model-training runs. Future work could extend our framework to broader research environments, including LM post-training, and evaluate its effectiveness in longer, end-to-end research campaigns.

7 Ethics Statement

This work studies the use of LLMs to automate research on language-model development. Such systems may help reduce the cost of experimentation and accelerate scientific progress, but they also introduce risks, including unreliable experimental conclusions, increased computational resource consumption, and the potential misuse of automated model-improvement capabilities. Our framework evaluates proposals in controlled training environments and uses real experimental outcomes to calibrate surrogate feedback. Nevertheless, predicted rewards and experimental gains do not guarantee the safety or broader usefulness of proposed model changes. We therefore emphasize the importance of human oversight, independent evaluation, and appropriate safeguards when applying automated research systems to more capable models or higher-stakes settings.

Appendix A More Details of Related Works

A.1 World Models for LLM Agents.

A world model predicts the consequences of an agent’s actions, enabling planning or learning without interacting with the real environment Sutton (1991); Ha and Schmidhuber (2018); Hafner et al. (2023). Recent work uses LLMs as world models for reasoning Hao et al. (2023), web navigation Chae et al. (2025); Gu et al. (2024), text-based simulation Wang et al. (2024), and agent training in synthetic environments Chen et al. (2026). In AutoResearch, concurrent work WMRL Yang et al. (2026b) uses a frozen LLM as the world model to predict execution outcomes as RL rewards and rescales them with a monotone mapping fitted on real executions at every training step. In contrast, LM2LM uses a frozen LLM as the world model that learns research knowledge from real experimental records in context Wang et al. (2026b), and improves its predictions on the current policy’s proposals by adding the outcomes of a few top-rated ones to these records.

A.2 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs

Reinforcement learning (RL) Shao et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2025); Yu et al. (2026); Lin et al. (2026a); Wu et al. (2026) has become an effective approach to improving LLM capabilities, particularly through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) Lambert et al. (2025). Methods such as GRPO Shao et al. (2024) and DAPO Yu et al. (2026) optimize LLM policies using group-relative feedback without a learned value function. While RLVR typically relies on inexpensive verification, such as checking mathematical answers or executing code, LM development requires costly model-training experiments to measure proposal quality. Recent work applies RL to automated AI research using execution feedback Yang et al. (2026a); Si et al. (2026), but obtaining rewards through real execution at every training step limits scalability. In contrast, LM2LM uses RWM-predicted experimental gains as RL rewards, while periodically calibrating the RWM with selected real executions to maintain feedback reliability.

A.3 Self-Evolving LLMs and Agents

Self-evolving methods improve a model or agent with data or feedback it generates itself. One line trains LLMs on self-generated solutions that are filtered or rewarded by verifiers or by the model itself Zelikman et al. (2022); Gulcehre et al. (2023); Yuan et al. (2024). Another line lets agents modify their own code, prompts, or workflows and keeps the changes that improve benchmark performance Lin et al. (2026b); Yin et al. (2025); Robeyns et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2026c); Lin et al. (2026d). These methods rely on feedback that is cheap to obtain, such as answer checking, code execution, or benchmark scores. In LM development, measuring a single proposal requires a full model-training run. LM2LM addresses this setting by learning from RWM-predicted gains and calibrating the RWM with a small number of real executions, and it targets the ability to improve LM development, which recursive self-improvement ultimately requires.

Appendix B Methodology Details of LM2LM

B.1 Reward Design

Reward Scale. The task-specific reward scale is τe=max⁡(σe, 1.4826​MADe)\tau_{e}=\max(\sigma_{e},\,1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}_{e}), where σe\sigma_{e} is the standard deviation of three reference runs and MADe\mathrm{MAD}_{e} is the median absolute deviation of the RWM-predicted gains for task ee from previous rollouts. It is recomputed at the start of each training segment and held fixed within the segment; for the first segment, MADe\mathrm{MAD}_{e} is estimated from RWM predictions on proposals of a preliminary run.

Validity, Repetition, and Bonuses. A proposal is valid if it can be translated into an executable modification of the task’s reference configuration, which is checked without running it. A proposal that changes nothing, i.e., all of whose modifications are inert, receives −3-3 instead of −c-c. Repetition is decided on the resolved implementation: a proposal repeats the reference configuration if it resolves to it, the history if it matches a proposal in hh, and an earlier proposal of its group if their implementations coincide. A proposal that repeats an earlier proposal of its own group keeps at most zero reward, and if no proposal of a group is valid and novel, every proposal of the group receives −c-c. In the rollouts whose proposals are selected for calibration, a valid proposal with a positive predicted gain also receives a novelty bonus 0.2​σG/1+Nprev0.2\,\sigma_{G}/\sqrt{1+N_{\mathrm{prev}}} in addition to the diversity bonus bib_{i}, where NprevN_{\mathrm{prev}} is the number of earlier occurrences of the same change on the task.

Hyperparameters. We use a repetition margin δ=1\delta=1 and a diversity weight λ=0.3\lambda=0.3.

B.2 Synthetic Training-State Expansion

Training states are initially constructed as described in Appendix C.2. After each rollout, i.e., every 8 training steps, we add the proposals generated in that rollout to the history pool, with their gains predicted by the current RWM as synthetic outcomes, and resample histories from the combined pool of real and predicted records to construct the training states of the next rollout.

B.3 Algorithm of LM2LM

Algorithm 1 summarizes the full training procedure of LM2LM.

Appendix C Environments and Data

C.1 Model Families

Each family shares an architecture, training-data distribution, and evaluation metric across its tasks.

AR Families.

  • •

    OLMo-3 Olmo et al. (2025): OLMo-3 small models trained on samples of Dolma 3 and evaluated by mean bits per byte (BPB) across ten downstream tasks (ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, four MMLU subsets, HumanEval, MBPP, and MATH-500).

  • •

    Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025): The official Qwen3 architecture and tokenizer. Training data (Dolma 3) and evaluation (ten-task BPB) are shared with OLMo-3.

  • •

    NanoChat Karpathy (2025): depth-parameterized transformers trained on ClimbMix and evaluated by BPB on a held-out ClimbMix validation shard.

  • •

    Marin Hall et al. (2025): Marin architectures with the same training data and evaluation as OLMo-3.

Diffusion Families. All four families are trained on SlimPajama with a 2,048-token context and evaluated by the negative log-likelihood of true tokens accumulated along the model’s greedy, most-confident-first unmasking order, measured in nats per token.

  • •

    E2D2 Arriola et al. (2026): an encoder-decoder masked diffusion model with a clean-token encoder and a cross-attention decoder for noisy tokens. Noise levels are sampled per block, yielding block-autoregressive modeling.

  • •

    E2D2-SW Wang et al. (2026a): This is an E2D2 variant with a token-causal encoder and a decoder trained on packed sliding windows of blocks but evaluated on non-overlapping blocks.

  • •

    BD3LM Arriola et al. (2025): a block diffusion model using a single network over concatenated clean and noisy sequences with block-structured attention.

  • •

    MDM Nie et al. (2025): a full-sequence bidirectional masked diffusion model with one noise level per sequence; it appears only among the training tasks and has no held-out task.

Tasks. A task specifies a model family, size, and training budget. Tasks within a family share the training data, tokenizer, evaluation protocol, and hardware. We construct tasks across these model families, following the naming conventions below:

  • •

    OLMo-3: 100m-1c denotes 100M non-embedding parameters trained with C=1C=1 times the Chinchilla-optimal budget Hoffmann et al. (2022), or 20​C20C tokens per parameter (2B tokens).

  • •

    Qwen3: Two model lines are kept separate. q152m-2b has 152.5M parameters, 2B training tokens, and an 8,192-token context. q06b-1b uses the official Qwen3-0.6B configuration with 1B training tokens and a 2,048-token context, appearing only in training tasks.

  • •

    NanoChat: d12-8k-2p15b denotes a depth-12 model (width 768) with an 8,192-token context trained on 2.15B tokens; p denotes the decimal point.

  • •

    Marin: 486m-8b denotes 485.9M parameters trained on 8B tokens; 2p9b denotes 2.9B tokens.

  • •

    Diffusion families: 113m-6e18 denotes 113M non-embedding parameters trained with 6×10186\times 10^{18} FLOPs, from which the token budget is derived.

Each task uses its family’s default training recipe as the reference configuration. The reference loss beb_{e} and seed noise σe\sigma_{e} are the mean and standard deviation of validation loss over three runs. Table 3 summarizes training tasks, held-out tasks and states, and available executed records by family. Table 4 details the held-out tasks, which differ from training tasks in model size or training budget.

C.2 Data Construction

Mechanism Library. We curate a library of training-recipe mechanisms covering model architecture, optimization, and training objectives. Each reviewed card specifies a hypothesis, expected effects, supporting evidence, and family-specific configurations (levels) with validity constraints. The AR library contains 40 accepted cards; Table 6 shows an example.

The library also defines the action space shared by all proposers, specifying modifiable recipe settings and their valid values. Proposals may combine any number of mechanisms, choose numerical values within valid ranges, and propose new variants for allowed categorical settings, which the builder implements. Model size, training budget, data, tokenizer, evaluation, seeds, and hardware remain fixed.

Experimental Records. We construct 300 proposal–outcome records across 40 training tasks. To ensure diversity and balanced coverage of mechanism directions, we sample proposals by instantiating one or two mechanism-card levels per proposal. Of the 300 executed proposals, 226 involve a single mechanism direction and 74 combine two (Table 5). We select 100 records as the initial RWM records M0M_{0}.

Training and Baseline Data. Each research state s=(e,h)s=(e,h) consists of a task ee and a history hh of proposals and their outcomes. Initial RL histories contain 0–8 task-matched real records sampled from M0M_{0}, and are expanded with RWM-predicted outcomes during RL (Appendix B.2). ICL baselines use up to 300 executed records as in-context examples. SFT uses 300 (s,a)(s,a) pairs constructed from these records, while RFT-Real retains the 114 pairs with positive measured gains.

Held-out States. We construct 60 AR and 18 diffusion research states from 10 held-out tasks. All states contain histories of real experimental outcomes and are fixed across methods. No held-out experimental records are used for proposer training, RWM grounding, or calibration.

Appendix D Evaluation Protocol

D.1 Metrics

We evaluate all proposers on the same fixed set of 60 autoregressive (AR) and 18 diffusion held-out research states. For each state, a proposer generates four proposals, which are implemented by the same builder and evaluated through real model-training experiments. Invalid or unchanged proposals receive zero gain, while negative gains are retained.

Validation Metrics. We measure model performance using:

  • •

    BPB (Bits per Byte): Average number of bits needed to encode each byte of text, enabling comparisons across tokenizers Gao et al. (2020). We use it for AR models, evaluated on held-out text as specified per family (Appendix C.1).

  • •

    NLL (Negative Log-Likelihood): Negative log-probability assigned to validation sequences. For diffusion models, we compute the exact negative log-likelihood of the true tokens accumulated along the model’s greedy, most-confident-first within-block unmasking order, with each revealed position set to the true token, reported in nats per token.

Lower values indicate better model performance.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate proposal quality using:

  • •

    Avg@4 / Best@4: Mean / maximum real gain among four proposals per state, averaged equally across states.

  • •

    Win rate: Fraction of states where one method achieves higher Avg@4 than another, with ties counted as 0.5.

  • •

    Neg.: Fraction of proposals with negative real gains.

Experimental gains are reported in 10−310^{-3} BPB (AR) and 10−210^{-2} nats per token (diffusion).

D.2 Cost Accounting

Hardware and Prices. All experiments, including baseline training and evaluation, RL training, experimental data collection, reference runs, and on-policy calibration, use NVIDIA B200 GPUs. GPU usage is priced at $14.208 per B200 GPU-hour11 1 https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/capacityblocks/pricing/. For GPT-6-sol RWM calls, token prices22 2 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-sol per million are $2 (uncached input), $0.20 (cached input), $2.50 (cache write), and $10 (output).

Data-Generation Cost. We measure cost as the GPU expenses of real experimental executions plus the token cost of RWM predictions. Real executions include those used to collect ICL records, fine-tuning data, initial RWM records, and on-policy calibration records, including failed runs. We estimate RWM prediction costs using the corresponding model’s token prices. We exclude proposer and builder inference, proposer fine-tuning, and shared research-state construction.

Data-Generation Time. We measure time as the sum of real-execution durations, assuming sequential execution, and RWM prediction time.

Appendix E Additional Implementation Details

E.1 Models and Prompts.

The proposer’s backbone is Qwen3.8-27B. The RWM, GPT-6-sol, is queried with a single API request per proposal at high reasoning effort, without tools. The builder, GPT-6-astra, runs as a Codex agent OpenAI (2025) (codex exec) at high reasoning effort. Tables 13, and 14 list the prompts of RWM, and builder, respectively.

E.2 RL Training

We use DAPO with asymmetric clipping (ϵlow=0.2\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}}=0.2, ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28), a token-level policy-gradient loss, and no KL or entropy regularization. For dynamic sampling, we sample 277 states and retain 256 per rollout; importance-sampling ratios are clipped at 2.0. Proposals are sampled at temperature 1.0 with a maximum of 20,000 generated tokens. Each rollout is followed by eight policy updates with a global batch size of 256. We use Adam (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98), weight decay 0.1, and an initial learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, multiplied by 0.7 after each training segment.

E.3 On-Policy Calibration

The candidates 𝒞u\mathcal{C}_{u} in Eq. (9) are the proposals sampled by the current proposer on training states whose outcomes are not yet in MuM_{u}; in practice, we spread the selected top-rated proposals across training tasks and states. Each selected proposal is executed once on its training task, and the three calibrations add B0=31B_{0}=31, B1=38B_{1}=38, and B2=31B_{2}=31 records. Calibration outcomes enter only the RWM records, not the histories of training states.

E.4 SFT and RFT-Real

Each SFT pair uses a record’s executed proposal as the target, and a state of the record’s own task whose history contains 0–7 other records of that task from the 300 records, chosen to diversify histories across pairs. RFT-Real keeps the 114 pairs whose measured gain is positive (76 AR and 38 diffusion). We train separate LoRA adapters for AR and diffusion tasks with the configuration in Table 12, and sample proposals with the same decoding settings as LM2LM.

Appendix F Additional Main Results

F.1 Per-Family Results

Tables 7 and 8 break the results down by model family, and gains vary across families:

  • •

    LM2LM attains the highest Avg@4 and Best@4 on OLMo-3, Qwen3, E2D2, and BD3LM and the highest Best@4 on Marin, but falls behind GPT-6-sol-ICL in Avg@4 on Marin and E2D2-SW and behind Base-ICL in Best@4 on E2D2-SW.

  • •

    Although its AR advantage is largest on Qwen3, LM2LM still achieves the highest AR Avg@4 and Best@4 when excluding Qwen3 (4.42 and 10.68, vs. at most 3.09 and 7.58).

  • •

    On NanoChat, headroom is limited: no method improves by more than about 2​σe2\sigma_{e} (Best@4 at most 1.23×10−31.23\times 10^{-3} BPB), and GPT-6-sol-ICL is the only method with a positive Avg@4.

These results show that LM2LM can bring a smaller open-weight model to frontier-level performance in proposing effective LM improvements.

F.2 Statistical Robustness

We express experimental gains in units of task-specific seed noise σe\sigma_{e}, defined as the standard deviation of the reference configuration’s validation loss over three runs. Table 9 reports Avg@4 and Best@4 in units of σe\sigma_{e}, the fraction of proposals with gains exceeding 2​σe2\sigma_{e}, and Avg@4 relative to the reference loss. On AR tasks, LM2LM achieves an Avg@4 of 7.29​σe7.29\sigma_{e}, compared with at most 4.91​σe4.91\sigma_{e} for the baselines. Moreover, 50.8%50.8\% of its proposals exceed 2​σe2\sigma_{e}, compared with 22.5%22.5\% for Base and 40.0%40.0\% for GPT-6-sol-ICL, while its Avg@4 corresponds to a 1.28%1.28\% reduction in reference loss.

Appendix G Cost Analysis

G.1 Data-Generation Cost

Fig. 6 reports Best@4 against data-generation cost and time, complementing the Avg@4 results in Fig. 3; Table 11 lists the underlying numbers. The trends match those of Avg@4: on AR tasks, LM2LM exceeds every baseline already before its first calibration (18.91 at $23.9k, vs. at most 16.54 at $60.0k) and saturates after the second calibration, whereas on diffusion tasks its Best@4 rises with each calibration and exceeds every baseline at M3M_{3} (9.93 vs. at most 8.50).

G.2 Total Cost

We further account for proposer training costs beyond data generation to assess the overall cost-effectiveness of LM2LM.

Table 10 reports the total costs, including RL training for LM2LM and fine-tuning for SFT and RFT-Real, while ICL requires no training. At step 96 (M3M_{3}), LM2LM incurs $40.1k in data-generation costs and $16.1k in RL training costs, totaling $56.1k. Despite its additional RL training cost, LM2LM remains cheaper than ICL with K=300K=300 ($60.0k), while achieving substantially higher Avg@4 on AR (17.06 vs. 6.15) and diffusion tasks (7.10 vs. 4.94).

Appendix H Case Studies: Impact of Calibration Strategies

Top-rated calibration executes the proposals that the RWM rates highest and RL is about to reinforce, whereas random calibration samples proposals regardless of their predicted gains. The following two cases illustrate how this difference affects RL on held-out AR families.

Delayed Correction of Overestimated Changes. M-UPD-72 is a NanoChat change to the number of tokens per optimizer update that the RWM overestimates: under M0M_{0}, it rewards the change with +0.7+0.7 to +0.9+0.9 in the training reward scale, whereas its real reward on held-out states is about −1.46-1.46 (Fig. 7). Top-rated calibration executes seven proposals applying it in the first update (after step 16), five of which degrade the reference configuration; the RWM then rewards the change with −1.66-1.66, and its share of NanoChat training proposals falls from a peak of 45% at step 24 to 8% by step 64. Random calibration executes none of them in the first update, so the RWM keeps rewarding the change until the second update (after step 40); lagging behind the reward, its share still peaks at 80% at step 48 and falls to 24% only by step 72. Both shares eventually drop below 3% by step 96, but random calibration spends substantially more training on a harmful change before correcting it.

Misleading Records from Random Selection. Random calibration can also add records that mislead the RWM. Its first batch contains an OLMo change that replaces local attention with an alternative token-mixing operator, which happens to improve its training task by 1.43%. With this record, the RWM starts rewarding the change (mean training reward rising from about −0.6-0.6 under M0M_{0} to +0.8+0.8 after the first update and +1.2+1.2 by step 96), and RL raises its share of OLMo training proposals from 4% to 16% (Fig. 8). On held-out OLMo states, the change accounts for 53% of the proposals at step 96, with a mean real gain of −16.4×10−3-16.4\times 10^{-3} BPB, lowering the OLMo Avg@4 from 7.39 under top-rated calibration to −6.37-6.37. Under top-rated calibration, the RWM keeps penalizing the change (−1.2-1.2 to −0.5-0.5), and its share stays below 5%.

Appendix I Additional In-depth Analysis

I.1 Diagnosing RWM Feedback Reliability

Feedback Metric. At each checkpoint, we execute the four proposals of each of the 60 held-out AR states, whose outcomes never enter the records. The static variant is scored by W⁡(M0)W(M_{0}) throughout, and LM2LM by the RWM in force: W⁡(M0)W(M_{0}) at step 16, W⁡(M1)W(M_{1}) at step 40, W⁡(M2)W(M_{2}) at steps 48 and 64, W⁡(M3)W(M_{3}) at step 96, and W⁡(M4)W(M_{4}) at step 128. Rewards follow the normalization and clipping used for RL training, clip⁡(g/τeff,±6)\mathrm{clip}(g/\tau_{\mathrm{eff}},\pm 6). For the proposals i=1,…,Gi=1,\dots,G of a state, let r^i\hat{r}_{i} and rir_{i} denote their predicted and real rewards, and let

A^i=r^i−1G​∑j=1Gr^j,Ai=ri−1G​∑j=1Grj\hat{A}_{i}=\hat{r}_{i}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\hat{r}_{j},\qquad A_{i}=r_{i}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r_{j}

be their predicted and real advantages, with G=4G=4 (states with fewer than two scored proposals are skipped). We use the following metrics, with 95% bootstrap intervals over states (2,000 resamples):

  • •

    Advantage cosine: the cosine similarity between the predicted and real advantages, concatenated over all states.

  • •

    Pairwise accuracy: over all pairs of proposals of a state whose real rewards differ, the fraction whose predicted order agrees with their real order, where a pair with equal predicted rewards counts as 0.5; pairs are pooled over states, so random rewards attain 0.5.

  • •

    Sign agreement: the fraction of proposals with nonzero A^i\hat{A}_{i} and AiA_{i} whose signs agree.

  • •

    Wrong-reinforcement rate: Pr⁡(Ai​<0∣A^i>​0)\Pr(A_{i}<0\mid\hat{A}_{i}>0), the fraction of positively reinforced proposals that perform below their group’s real mean.

  • •

    Top-1 hit rate: over states whose real rewards differ, the fraction in which the proposal with the highest predicted reward also has the highest real reward.

  • •

    Real advantage of reinforced proposals: the mean AiA_{i} over proposals with A^i>0\hat{A}_{i}>0.

We also report the mean predicted and real rewards and their difference (Fig. 5(c)).

Results. Fig. 9 complements the advantage alignment and ranking results of Sec. 4.5 by examining whether individual proposals are reinforced in the correct direction. Early in training, the static RWM provides feedback comparable to that of LM2LM, but its reliability deteriorates as the proposer evolves. From step 16 to step 64, its sign agreement drops from 0.78 to 0.52 and its wrong-reinforcement rate rises from 18% to 46%, reaching 0.43 and 55% at step 128. In contrast, the sign agreement of LM2LM is 0.68, 0.65, and 0.62 at steps 16, 64, and 128, and its wrong-reinforcement rate stays between 30% and 36% at these steps. As a result, the proposals that the static RWM reinforces have a negative mean real advantage from step 96 onward (−0.31-0.31), i.e., RL increasingly favors proposals that underperform their group, whereas those reinforced by LM2LM remain positive (0.18 to 0.59). Fig. 11 shows the same trend at the level of individual proposals.

I.2 Effect of Updating Records on Identical Proposals

The comparison in Sec. 4.5 involves two proposers that diverge during training. To isolate the effect of the records, we score the same proposals of LM2LM with the initial records M0M_{0} and with the calibrated records. With M0M_{0}, the pairwise accuracy drops to 0.49 at step 64, 0.46 at step 96, and 0.44 at step 128, whereas with the calibrated records it is 0.64 with M2M_{2} at step 64, 0.61 with M3M_{3} at step 96, and 0.61 with M4M_{4} at step 128 (Fig. 10). Since the proposals are identical, these differences come from the records alone.

I.3 Case Studies

Family-dependent optimizer changes. The RWM rewards an orthogonalized-momentum optimizer with +1.0+1.0 to +2.0+2.0 on OLMo-3 and Qwen3 training tasks but with −2-2 to −3-3 on NanoChat. The proposer follows this feedback: the share of the change in its OLMo-3 proposals rises from 7% to 78%, while on NanoChat it drops to 0%. Real execution confirms both decisions: on held-out states, the change improves 93% of the OLMo-3 and 100% of the Qwen3 proposals that apply it, by up to 21.6×10−321.6\times 10^{-3} BPB on a single OLMo-3 state, whereas on NanoChat, where Base proposes it, it loses 44×10−344\times 10^{-3} BPB on average.

Correction of misleading rewards. M-UPD-72 changes the number of tokens per optimizer update on NanoChat (Fig. 12). M0M_{0} contains no record of it, and the RWM rewards it with +0.7+0.7 to +1.25+1.25, whereas its real reward on held-out states is about −1.46-1.46. Both variants start with about 30% of their NanoChat training proposals applying it; the static variant concentrates on it, reaching 79% of its NanoChat training and held-out proposals by step 64. The first calibration of LM2LM executes seven such proposals, five of which degrade the reference configuration; afterwards the RWM rewards the change with −1.66-1.66, close to its real reward, and its share falls to 8% in training and 7% on held-out states by step 64, after growing until step 24 as the proposer lags behind the reward. On held-out NanoChat states, LM2LM ends with an Avg@4 of −1.89-1.89 at step 96, compared with −10.84-10.84 for the static variant, and outperforms it on all 17 states.

We used an OpenAI LLM (GPT-6.1) as a writing and formatting assistant. In particular, it helped refine grammar and phrasing, improve clarity, and suggest edits to figure/table captions and layout (e.g., column alignment, caption length, placement). The LLM did not contribute to research ideation, experimental design, implementation, data analysis, or technical content beyond surface-level edits. All outputs were reviewed and edited by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final text and visuals.
